claim: Homozygous rps-18(ok3353) mutants exhibited early larval arrest.
source: Homozygous rps-18(ok3353) mutants (rps-18(0), Figure 1A) exhibited early larval arrest.
evidence: Direct statement in the text describing the phenotype of the mutant.

claim: Homozygous rpl-29(tm3555) mutants were superficially wild type.
source: On the other hand, homozygous rpl-29(tm3555) mutants (rpl-29(0), Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) were superficially wild type, reflecting a possible non-essential role of rpl-29 in ribosome function.
evidence: Direct observation of mutant phenotype reported in the text.

claim: Single-copy transgene juSi83[Prps-18-GFP::rps-18] rescued the rps-18(0) early larval arrest but did not rescue sterility.
source: Our single-copy transgene juSi83[Prps-18-GFP::rps-18] (Figure 1A) rescued the rps-18(0) early larval arrest, but did not rescue sterility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), despite visible GFP expression in the germline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, gonad).
evidence: Experimental data showing partial rescue of mutant phenotype.

claim: Large fluorescent tags partly impaired RPS-18 function.
source: Tagging with other fluorescent tags, such as mEOS, Dendra, and mini Singlet Oxygen Generator (miniSOG), also failed to fully rescue rps-18(0) phenotypes (data not shown), suggesting that large tags partly impaired RPS-18 function.
evidence: Inference from failure to rescue phenotypes with various fluorescent tags.

claim: GFP::RPS-18 was observed in the cytosol appearing as reticular structures in rescued somatic tissues.
source: In the rescued somatic tissues, we observed GFP::RPS-18 in the cytosol, appearing as reticular structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Direct microscopy observation reported in text and shown in figure.

claim: RPL-29::GFP expressed from a single-copy transgene showed a similar localization pattern to GFP::RPS-18.
source: RPL-29::GFP expressed from a single-copy transgene (juSi123[Prpl-29-rpl-29::GFP]) in the rpl-29(0) background showed a similar pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Comparison of localization patterns between two ribosomal proteins.

claim: Most of the GFP::RPS-18 and RPL-29::GFP signals represent assembled ribosomes as opposed to unassembled proteins or subunits.
source: The similarity in localization of these large and small subunit proteins suggests that most of the signals represent assembled ribosomes as opposed to unassembled proteins or subunits.
evidence: Inference based on similar localization patterns of large and small ribosomal subunit proteins.

claim: Expression from single-copy transgenes of GFP::RPS-18 or RPL-29::GFP caused no detectable defects.
source: Importantly, the expression from these single-copy transgenes caused no detectable defects (data not shown) unlike the overexpression of rps-18 or rpl-29.
evidence: Observation that single-copy expression does not cause phenotypic defects.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of Prps-18-GFP::RPS-18 was significantly lower in the rps-18(+)/rps-18(+) or rps-18(+)/rps-18(0) background than in homozygous rps-18(0)/rps-18(0) mutants.
source: We observed that the fluorescence intensity of Prps-18-GFP::RPS-18 was significantly lower in the rps-18(+)/rps-18(+) or rps-18(+)/rps-18(0) background than in homozygous rps-18(0)/rps-18(0) mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements across different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Prpl-29-GFP::rpl-29 signal intensity depended on the endogenous rpl-29 locus.
source: Similarly, Prpl-29-GFP::rpl-29 signal intensity depended on the endogenous rpl-29 locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Quantitative data showing signal intensity varies with endogenous gene copy number.

claim: Negative feedback regulation eliminates excess ribosomal proteins.
source: These results suggest that negative feedback regulation eliminates excess ribosomal proteins, similar to that previously reported in bacteria (Kaczanowska and Rydén-Aulin, 2007).
evidence: Inference from expression data and comparison to known bacterial mechanisms.

claim: The null mutant background is necessary to obtain sufficiently bright signals for visualization of GFP-tagged ribosomal proteins.
source: Therefore, the null mutant background is necessary to obtain sufficiently bright signals for visualization of GFP-tagged ribosomal proteins.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from fluorescence intensity data in different genetic backgrounds.

claim: A single-copy expression of GFP11::RPS-18 (juSi94[GFP11::rps-18]) completely rescued larval arrest and sterility of rps-18(0).
source: Importantly, we found that a single-copy expression of GFP11::RPS-18 (juSi94[GFP11::rps-18]) completely rescued larval arrest and sterility of rps-18(0) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental data showing complete rescue of mutant phenotypes.

claim: GFP11 is much smaller (16 amino acids) compared to GFP (237 amino acids).
source: This is probably because GFP11 is much smaller (16 amino acids), compared to GFP (237 amino acids), supporting our interpretation for partial impaired function of the GFP::RPS-18.
evidence: Established knowledge about the sizes of GFP11 and GFP.

claim: The subcellular fluorescence pattern revealed by the split-GFP transgenic approach was similar to that from the single-copy expression of GFP::RPS-18 or of RPL-29::GFP.
source: Nonetheless, the subcellular fluorescence pattern revealed by this split-GFP transgenic approach was similar to that from the single-copy expression of GFP::RPS-18 or of RPL-29::GFP.
evidence: Comparison of fluorescence patterns between different labeling approaches.

claim: In adult epidermis-specific Pcol-19-RIBOS, signals were observed in the epidermal cytosol excluded from reticular structures.
source: In adult epidermis-specific Pcol-19-RIBOS, we observed signals in the epidermal cytosol excluded from reticular structures (Figure 1C, Epidermis).
evidence: Direct microscopy observation of RIBOS signals in epidermis.

claim: Although RPS-18 is expressed in the whole body, fluorescence was not observed in any other tissues such as intestine in Pcol-19-RIBOS.
source: Although RPS-18 is expressed in the whole body, fluorescence was not observed in any other tissues, such as intestine (Figure 1C, Intestine), suggesting that GFPP11::RPS-18 did not have fluorescence.
evidence: Observation that fluorescence is tissue-specific despite ubiquitous expression of GFP11::RPS-18.

claim: Worms expressing Pcol-19-GFP1-10 transgene alone did not show fluorescent signals compared to Pcol-19-RIBOS.
source: Worms expressing Pcol-19-GFP1-10 transgene alone also did not show fluorescent signals compared to Pcol-19-RIBOS (Figure 1C and Materials and Methods).
evidence: Negative control experiment showing GFP1-10 alone does not produce fluorescence.

claim: Photobleached GFP11::RPS-18 showed a longer recovery time and smaller mobile fraction than IFE-2::GFP and IFE-4::GFP.
source: Photobleached GFP11::RPS-18 showed a longer recovery time and smaller mobile fraction than IFE-2::GFP and IFE-4::GFP (Figure 1F–1H).
evidence: FRAP experimental data comparing recovery kinetics.

claim: The recovery curve, t1/2, and mobile fraction of GFP11::RPS-18 were comparable to that of the ribosomal large subunit, RPL-29::GFP.
source: Furthermore, the recovery curve, t1/2, and mobile fraction of GFP11::RPS-18 were comparable to that of the ribosomal large subunit, RPL-29::GFP (Figure 1F–1H), suggesting that fluorescence recovery was not affected by splitting GFP, and that RPS-18 and RPL-29 were incorporated into a complex with a similar mobility, likely the ribosome.
evidence: FRAP data comparison between small and large ribosomal subunits.

claim: Body wall muscle-specific Pmyo-3-RIBOS revealed that fluorescence was observed in the muscle arm besides strong somatic signals.
source: Body wall muscle-specific Pmyo-3-RIBOS revealed that besides strong somatic signals, fluorescence was observed in the muscle arm (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), an elaborate postsynaptic structure extending to the nerve cord to receive inputs from presynaptic neurons (Dixon and Roy, 2005).
evidence: Microscopy observation of RIBOS signals in muscle tissue.

claim: RIBOS signals in muscle arms were consistent with the distribution of ribosomes in muscle arms as found in electron micrographs.
source: Such RIBOS signals were consistent with the distribution of ribosomes in muscle arms as found in electron micrographs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Correlation between fluorescence microscopy and electron microscopy data.

claim: Pan-neuronal Prgef-1-RIBOS showed that ribosomes were mostly restricted to the soma.
source: Pan-neuronal Prgef-1-RIBOS showed that ribosomes were mostly restricted to the soma (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Microscopy observation of ribosome distribution in neurons.

claim: Initiation factors IFE-2::GFP and IFE-4::GFP were diffuse in cell bodies and nerve processes in the ventral nerve cord.
source: In contrast to the restricted signals of ribosomes, initiation factors IFE-2::GFP and IFE-4::GFP were diffuse in cell bodies and nerve processes in the ventral nerve cord (Figure 2C).
evidence: Microscopy observation comparing ribosome and initiation factor localization.

claim: STAU-1 formed two foci in the soma.
source: STAU-1 (LeGendre et al., 2013), an ortholog of Staufen, formed two foci in the soma; AIN-1 (ALG-1-interacting protein-1), an ortholog of GW182 (Ding et al., 2005), formed puncta in the soma and along the neuronal processes (Figure 2C).
evidence: Microscopy observation of RNA granule component localization.

claim: AIN-1 formed puncta in the soma and along the neuronal processes.
source: STAU-1 (LeGendre et al., 2013), an ortholog of Staufen, formed two foci in the soma; AIN-1 (ALG-1-interacting protein-1), an ortholog of GW182 (Ding et al., 2005), formed puncta in the soma and along the neuronal processes (Figure 2C).
evidence: Microscopy observation of RNA granule component localization.

claim: Neither the initiation factors nor the RNA granule components showed localization similar to ribosomes.
source: Neither the initiation factors nor the RNA granule components showed localization similar to ribosomes, implying that protein translation-related components might be differentially regulated in their localization.
evidence: Comparison of localization patterns between different translation-related components.

claim: In the first larval (L1) stage, ribosomes colocalized with presynaptic markers, RAB-3, in the ventral cord, corresponding to the presynaptic terminals of DD motor neurons.
source: In the first larval (L1) stage, we found that ribosomes colocalized with presynaptic markers, RAB-3, in the ventral cord, corresponding to the presynaptic terminals of DD motor neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: Colocalization analysis of RIBOS signals with presynaptic markers.

claim: From L2 to older larvae, Punc-25-RIBOS signals in the ventral cord were excluded from VD presynaptic terminals.
source: From L2 to older larvae, we observed Punc-25-RIBOS signals in the ventral cord, which were excluded from VD presynaptic terminals (Figure 3A).
evidence: Microscopy observation of ribosome localization relative to presynaptic terminals.

claim: DD neuron-specific Pflp-13-RIBOS showed similar localization to Punc-25-RIBOS.
source: DD neuron-specific Pflp-13-RIBOS showed similar localization (Figure 3B), suggesting that ribosome localization was changed from presynaptic to postsynaptic compartments in the DD neurons.
evidence: Comparison of RIBOS signals in different neuron-specific markers.

claim: Reconstruction of serial EM sections showed that the number of ribosomes in DD axonal profiles was higher at the L1 stage than the adult stage.
source: Consistent with RIBOS, reconstruction of serial EM sections showed that the number of ribosomes in DD axonal profiles was higher at the L1 stage than the adult stage (Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantitative electron microscopy data comparing ribosome numbers across developmental stages.

claim: Ribosomes were observed in the presynaptic terminals of adult VD neurons in serial EM sections.
source: In the adult presynaptic terminals, the evidence of ribosome localization has been limited (Akins et al., 2009). Here, we observed ribosomes in the presynaptic terminals of adult VD neurons in serial EM sections (Figure 3C).
evidence: Electron microscopy observation of ribosomes in presynaptic terminals.

claim: Using electron tomography, the existence of ribosomes in the presynaptic terminals of VD neurons was confirmed.
source: Using electron tomography, we further confirmed the existence of ribosomes in the presynaptic terminals of those neurons (Figure 3D and E), based on the following criteria: ribosomes in neurons had spherical shapes with 20 nm diameter, and resembled ribosomes in muscles (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: Electron tomography data confirming ribosome presence based on morphological criteria.

claim: RIBOS signals in the ventral cord colocalized with presynaptic markers could not be detected at the adult stage, likely due to the number of ribosomes being below the light microscopy detection threshold.
source: We were unable to detect RIBOS signals in the ventral cord colocalized with presynaptic markers at the adult stage, likely due to the number of ribosomes being below that of light microscopy detection threshold.
evidence: Inference from inability to detect fluorescence despite EM evidence of ribosomes.

claim: In mechanosensory neurons, ribosomes were observed in the soma and the proximal axon (~20 µm from the soma).
source: In these neurons, we observed ribosomes in the soma and the proximal axon (~20 µm from the soma, Figure 4A).
evidence: Microscopy observation of ribosome distribution in mechanosensory neurons.

claim: Ribosomes formed puncta along the axon and puncta density decreased from L1 to adult stage in PLM neurons.
source: Ribosomes also formed puncta along the axon and puncta density decreased from L1 to adult stage in PLM neurons (Figure 4A–4C).
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data showing developmental changes in ribosome puncta density.

claim: At the L1 stage, but not at the adult stage, ribosome puncta were associated with the junction of the synaptic branch of PLM neurons.
source: At the L1 stage, but not at the adult stage, these puncta were associated with the junction of the synaptic branch of PLM neurons (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: Microscopy observation comparing ribosome localization at different developmental stages.

claim: Ribosomal localization changes during neuronal development.
source: These data indicate that ribosomal localization changes during the neuronal development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from developmental time course data.

claim: In C. elegans mechanosensory neurons, local translation in axons is induced after axon injury.
source: In C. elegans mechanosensory neurons, local translation in axons is induced after axon injury (Yan et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation of previous research on local translation after injury.

claim: Axon regrowth partly depended on new protein synthesis because treatment with cycloheximide inhibited this regrowth.
source: Axon regrowth partly depended on new protein synthesis because treatment with cycloheximide, which blocks protein synthesis, inhibited this regrowth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data showing drug treatment effect on axon regrowth.

claim: One hour after axon injury, ribosome accumulation began at the injured site of the proximal axon and appeared to plateau after three hours.
source: One hour after axon injury, ribosome accumulation began at the injured site of the proximal axon and appeared to plateau after three hours (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Time course microscopy data showing ribosome accumulation after injury.

claim: Weak RIBOS signals were observed in the regrowing tip after axon injury.
source: We also observed weak RIBOS signals in the regrowing tip (Figure 5A).
evidence: Microscopy observation of ribosomes in regrowing axons.

claim: Negative controls involving no wounding or laser wounding without severing the axon did not induce ribosome accumulation.
source: Negative controls involving no wounding or laser wounding without severing the axon did not induce ribosome accumulation (Figure 5B).
evidence: Control experiments showing specificity of ribosome accumulation to axon injury.

claim: Reconstruction of EM serial sections showed accumulation of electron-dense monosomes at the cutting site six hours after axotomy.
source: Consistent with RIBOS, reconstruction of EM serial sections showed accumulation of electron-dense monosomes at the cutting site six hours after axotomy (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Electron microscopy data confirming ribosome accumulation after injury.

claim: Mitochondria were observed around the cutting site in the EM images after axotomy.
source: We also observed mitochondria around the cutting site in the EM images (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Electron microscopy observation of mitochondria at injury site.

claim: The uninjured axon contained no ribosomes or mitochondria.
source: The uninjured axon contained no ribosomes or mitochondria (Figure 5C).
evidence: Electron microscopy observation of uninjured axons as control.

claim: Axonal ribosomes at the adult stage can alter their localization after axon injury.
source: These results suggest that axonal ribosomes at the adult stage can alter their localization after axon injury.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RIBOS and EM data after axon injury.

claim: Loss-of-function mutants of C. elegans orthologs for ankyrin (unc-44) and spectrin (unc-70) showed normal ribosome distribution in the soma and axon.
source: We found normal ribosome distribution in the soma and axon in loss-of-function mutants of C. elegans orthologs for ankyrin (unc-44) and its putative binding partner spectrin (unc-70) (Figure 6), indicating that these genes may not play a role in restricting ribosomes in the soma.
evidence: Genetic analysis showing no effect of ankyrin and spectrin mutants on ribosome distribution.

claim: In PLM neurons of unc-16 mutants, ribosomes were decreased in the proximal axon and increased in the presynaptic terminals without affecting somatic distribution.
source: In PLM neurons of unc-16 mutants, ribosomes were decreased in the proximal axon and increased in the presynaptic terminals without affecting somatic distribution (Figure 6), suggesting that UNC-16 acted as a gatekeeper for ribosomes in mechanosensory neurons.
evidence: Genetic analysis showing altered ribosome distribution in unc-16 mutants.

claim: Eight mutants displaying aberrant ribosomal distribution were found in a forward genetic screen using Pmec-4-RIBOS.
source: Thus, we performed a genetic screen using Pmec-4-RIBOS and found eight mutants displaying aberrant ribosomal distribution (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Results from forward genetic screen.

claim: Ribosomes in the eight mutants accumulated in the cell cortex and around the nucleus, compared to the relatively diffused distribution in the wild type, and increased in the proximal axon with partial penetrance.
source: Ribosomes in these mutants accumulated in the cell cortex and around the nucleus, compared to the relatively diffused distribution in the wild type, and increased in the proximal axon with partial penetrance (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Microscopy observation of ribosome distribution in mutants from genetic screen.

claim: All eight mutants had misshapen mechanosensory neuron cell bodies and insensitivity to gentle touch.
source: In addition to these ribosome defects, all mutants had misshapen mechanosensory neuron cell bodies, and insensitivity to gentle touch.
evidence: Phenotypic characterization of mutants from genetic screen.

claim: All mutations from the genetic screen affect tubulin or tubulin regulatory genes, previously isolated as mechanosensory abnormality (mec) genes.
source: Based on complementation tests and sequencing, we found that all mutations affect tubulin or tubulin regulatory genes, previously isolated as mechanosensory abnormality (mec) genes (Table 1).
evidence: Genetic mapping and sequencing results identifying mutated genes.

claim: Four recessive mutations (ju1286, ju1287, ju1294, and ju1298) and a dominant mutation ju1297 affecting ribosome localization were found to be substitution mutations in mec-7.
source: Four recessive mutations (ju1286, ju1287, ju1294, and ju1298) and a dominant mutation ju1297 affecting ribosome localization were found to be substitution mutations in mec-7 (Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Sequencing data identifying specific mutations in mec-7.

claim: All four recessive mutations in mec-7 are located in the exchangeable GDP/GTP-binding site of the dimer-dimer interface of α- and β-tubulins.
source: All four recessive mutations are located in the exchangeable GDP/GTP-binding site of the dimer-dimer interface of α- and β-tubulins (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, magenta).
evidence: Structural analysis mapping mutations to protein structure.

claim: The dominant mutation ju1297 in mec-7 is located in the non-exchangeable GTP-binding site of the monomer-monomer interface.
source: In contrast, the dominant mutation is located in the non-exchangeable GTP-binding site of the monomer-monomer interface (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, cyan).
evidence: Structural analysis mapping mutation to protein structure.

claim: One dominant allele, ju1295, was mapped to mec-12 and caused a Glu to Ser substitution on the exchangeable GDP/GTP-binding site in the dimer-dimer interface.
source: One dominant allele, ju1295, was mapped to mec-12 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) and caused a Glu to Ser substitution on the exchangeable GDP/GTP-binding site in the dimer-dimer interface (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, light green).
evidence: Genetic mapping and sequencing identifying mutation in mec-12.

claim: A deletion allele mec-7(u443) and a recessive loss-of-function allele of mec-12(e1607) exhibited comparable ribosome distribution defects.
source: A deletion allele mec-7(u443) and a recessive loss-of-function allele of mec-12(e1607) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, light blue) exhibited comparable ribosome distribution defects (Figure 7D), suggesting that the identified mutations were causative.
evidence: Genetic analysis comparing different alleles to confirm causality.

claim: Dominant alleles, mec-7(ju1297) and mec-12(ju1295) showed lower penetrance of ribosome defects than recessive alleles of mec-7 only in the axons.
source: Interestingly, dominant alleles, mec-7(ju1297) and mec-12(ju1295) showed lower penetrance of ribosome defects than recessive alleles of mec-7 only in the axons (Figure 7B).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of phenotype penetrance between different alleles.

claim: Axonal and somatic ribosomes might be differentially regulated.
source: This result suggests that axonal and somatic ribosomes might be differentially regulated.
evidence: Inference from differential penetrance of phenotypes in different cellular compartments.

claim: Two recessive mutations, ju1288 and ju1289, were mapped to the E3 ubiquitin ligase homolog, mec-15.
source: Two recessive mutations, ju1288 and ju1289, were mapped to the E3 ubiquitin ligase homolog, mec-15 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), which regulates expression of mec-7 and mec-12 genes (Bounoutas et al., 2009b; Gu et al., 1996).
evidence: Genetic mapping identifying mutations in mec-15.

claim: A mutant of the α-tubulin acetyltransferase, mec-17, showed similar ribosome distribution defects.
source: We then tested a mutant of the α-tubulin acetyltransferase, mec-17 (Akella et al., 2010), and found that it showed similar ribosome distribution defects (Figure 7D).
evidence: Genetic analysis of mec-17 mutant showing ribosome distribution phenotype.

claim: Tubulin genes and their regulation are important for ribosome distribution.
source: These results suggest that tubulin genes and their regulation are important for ribosome distribution.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic analysis of multiple tubulin-related genes.

claim: mec-4 and mec-2 mutants did not show ribosome distribution defects.
source: In contrast to the tubulin genes, mec-4 and mec-2 mutants did not show ribosome distribution defects (Figure 7D).
evidence: Genetic analysis showing no effect of mechanosensory channel and adaptor mutants.

claim: mec-12(e1605) mutants, which are mechanosensory defective but have intact microtubules, did not show ribosome distribution defects.
source: Furthermore, mec-12(e1605) mutants, which are mechanosensory defective but have intact microtubules (Bounoutas et al., 2009a), did not show ribosome distribution defects (Figure 7D).
evidence: Genetic analysis separating mechanosensory function from microtubule structure.

claim: Ribosome distribution defects are not a direct consequence of mechanosensory defects.
source: Together, these results suggest that ribosome distribution defects are not a direct consequence of mechanosensory defects.
evidence: Conclusion from genetic analysis of mechanosensory mutants without ribosome defects.

claim: Chronic colchicine treatment from eggs induced ribosome distribution defects similar to mec-7 or mec-12 mutants.
source: Chronic treatment from eggs induced ribosome distribution defects similar to mec-7 or mec-12 mutants, suggesting that filamentous microtubules, but not globular tubulins, were important (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, Egg).
evidence: Drug treatment experiment disrupting microtubules.

claim: Acute colchicine treatment at the L4 or young adult stage altered ribosome somatic distribution.
source: Acute treatment at the L4 or young adult stage altered ribosome somatic distribution (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Drug treatment experiment at specific developmental stages.

claim: Somatic defects emerged at the adult stage in mec-7 mutants.
source: Also, somatic defects emerged at the adult stage in mec-7 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Developmental time course analysis of mutant phenotypes.

claim: Microtubules are important for the maintenance of ribosome distribution in the soma.
source: These results suggest that microtubules are important for the maintenance of ribosome distribution in the soma.
evidence: Conclusion from drug treatment and developmental analysis.

claim: Axonal defects were not induced by acute colchicine treatment.
source: In contrast, axonal defects were not induced by acute colchicine treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) and emerged at the larval stage in the mec-7 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that microtubules might be important for the generation of a barrier in the proximal axon.
evidence: Drug treatment and developmental analysis showing differential effects on axons vs soma.

claim: The observation of polysomes in the base of dendritic spines in rat dentate gyrus neurons provided crucial early evidence for local translation in neurons.
source: The observation of polysomes in the base of dendritic spines in rat dentate gyrus neurons provided crucial early evidence for local translation in neurons (Steward and Levy, 1982).
evidence: Citation of historical evidence for local translation.

claim: Aberrant local protein synthesis disrupts neuronal plasticity in models for neurodevelopmental disorders, such as Tuberous sclerosis (TSC) and Fragile X syndrome (FXS).
source: Aberrant local protein synthesis disrupts neuronal plasticity in models for neurodevelopmental disorders, such as Tuberous sclerosis (TSC) and Fragile X syndrome (FXS) (Auerbach et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation of research on local translation in disease models.

claim: Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II α(CaMKIIα) mRNA is localized to dendrites via a cis regulatory element in its 3'-UTR.
source: For example, Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II α(CaMKIIα) mRNA is localized to dendrites via a cis regulatory element in its 3'-UTR, and removal of this element impairs long-term potentiation (LTP) and spatial memory (Miller et al., 2002);
evidence: Citation of research on mRNA localization and its functional importance.

claim: Removal of the 3'-UTR regulatory element of CaMKIIα mRNA impairs long-term potentiation (LTP) and spatial memory.
source: For example, Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II α(CaMKIIα) mRNA is localized to dendrites via a cis regulatory element in its 3'-UTR, and removal of this element impairs long-term potentiation (LTP) and spatial memory (Miller et al., 2002);
evidence: Citation of functional consequences of disrupting mRNA localization.

claim: β-actin mRNA is localized to the growing tip of an axon, the growth cone.
source: β-actin mRNA is localized to the growing tip of an axon, the growth cone, where its polarized translation is important for growth cone turning towards an attractant (Leung et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation of research on β-actin mRNA localization.

claim: Polarized translation of β-actin mRNA is important for growth cone turning towards an attractant.
source: β-actin mRNA is localized to the growing tip of an axon, the growth cone, where its polarized translation is important for growth cone turning towards an attractant (Leung et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation of functional importance of localized translation.

claim: Dendritic ribosomes associated with the netrin receptor, Deleted in Colorectal Cancer (DCC), are stalled and inactive, and released upon netrin signaling.
source: One striking example of ribosome localization is that dendritic ribosomes associated with the netrin receptor, Deleted in Colorectal Cancer (DCC), are stalled and inactive, and released upon netrin signaling (Tcherkezian et al., 2010).
evidence: Citation of research on regulated ribosome activity.

claim: Electron microscopy (EM) studies have long provided essential evidence for ribosomes, beginning with the discovery of ~20 nm diameter electron-dense particles rich in nucleic acids.
source: Electron microscopy (EM) studies have long provided essential evidence for ribosomes, beginning with the discovery of ~20 nm diameter electron-dense particles rich in nucleic acids (Palade, 1955).
evidence: Citation of historical EM studies of ribosomes.

claim: Individual ribosomes (monosomes) are attached to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or free in the cytosol.
source: Individual ribosomes (monosomes) are attached to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or free in the cytosol, while mRNA-bound polysomes appear as beaded strings in EM images.
evidence: Established knowledge about ribosome localization and appearance in EM.

claim: mRNA-bound polysomes appear as beaded strings in EM images.
source: Individual ribosomes (monosomes) are attached to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or free in the cytosol, while mRNA-bound polysomes appear as beaded strings in EM images.
evidence: Established knowledge about polysome appearance in EM.

claim: Clustered ribosomes, often termed plaques, have been identified in squid neurons, goldfish Mauthner cell axons, and mammalian peripheral axons.
source: These methods have been used to identify clustered ribosomes, often termed plaques, in squid neurons (Martin et al., 1998), goldfish Mauthner cell axons (Koenig and Martin, 1996), and mammalian peripheral axons (Koenig et al., 2000).
evidence: Citation of EM studies identifying ribosome clusters in various organisms.

claim: Overexpression of ribosomal subunit S29 causes apoptosis in primary cultured thymocytes of rats.
source: For example, overexpression of ribosomal subunit S29 causes apoptosis in primary cultured thymocytes of rats (Khanna et al., 2000).
evidence: Citation of research showing cellular defects from ribosomal protein overexpression.

claim: In bacteria, endogenous ribosomal protein S2 has been labeled with YFP.
source: In bacteria, endogenous ribosomal protein S2 has been labeled with YFP (Bakshi et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation of ribosome labeling in bacteria.

claim: In yeasts, endogenous loci of ribosomal proteins have been tagged with GFP.
source: In yeasts, endogenous loci of ribosomal proteins have been tagged with GFP (Huh et al., 2003).
evidence: Citation of ribosome labeling in yeast.

claim: In mice, knock-in of HA-tagged RPL22 has been used for ribosomal profiling of translational status.
source: For multicellular organisms, such as mice, knock-in of HA-tagged RPL22 (Sanz et al., 2009) or BAC transgenic expression of eGFP-tagged RPL10a (Heiman et al., 2008) has been used for ribosomal profiling of translational status.
evidence: Citation of ribosome labeling approaches in mice.

claim: BAC transgenic expression of eGFP-tagged RPL10a in mice has been used for ribosomal profiling of translational status.
source: For multicellular organisms, such as mice, knock-in of HA-tagged RPL22 (Sanz et al., 2009) or BAC transgenic expression of eGFP-tagged RPL10a (Heiman et al., 2008) has been used for ribosomal profiling of translational status.
evidence: Citation of ribosome labeling approaches in mice.

claim: HA-tagged RPL22 and eGFP-tagged RPL10a reagents do not allow direct visualization of endogenous ribosomes in living tissues.
source: However, these reagents do not allow direct visualization of endogenous ribosomes in living tissues.
evidence: Statement about limitations of existing reagents.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) is ideally suited for visualizing protein and organelle localization in vivo because it is transparent and genetically tractable.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) is ideally suited for visualizing protein and organelle localization in vivo because it is transparent and genetically tractable.
evidence: Established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton and the JIP3 protein UNC-16 exert distinct effects on localization of axonal and somatic ribosomes.
source: By examining mutants affecting axonal trafficking and performing a forward genetic screen, we showed that the microtubule cytoskeleton and the JIP3 protein UNC-16 exert distinct effects on localization of axonal and somatic ribosomes.
evidence: Summary of genetic analysis results.

claim: UNC-16 and microtubules have specific roles in neuronal ribosome localization.
source: Our data demonstrate the utility of tissue-specific visualization of ribosomes in vivo, and provide insight into the mechanisms of active regulation of ribosome localization in neurons.
evidence: Summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Overexpression of tagged ribosomal proteins caused abnormal morphologies of axons and cell bodies.
source: However, we noticed that such overexpression caused a variety of cellular defects, such as abnormal morphologies of axons and cell bodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and aggregates of ribosomal proteins in the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Observation of cellular defects from overexpression experiments.

claim: Overexpression of tagged ribosomal proteins caused aggregates of ribosomal proteins in the nucleus.
source: However, we noticed that such overexpression caused a variety of cellular defects, such as abnormal morphologies of axons and cell bodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and aggregates of ribosomal proteins in the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Observation of protein aggregation from overexpression experiments.

claim: When GFP1-10 and GFP11 coexist, they irreversibly assemble and produce green fluorescence.
source: To circumvent these challenges, we devised a strategy using self-assembling split GFP; when the first ten β-strands (GFP1-10) and the last β-strand (GFP11) coexist, they irreversibly assemble and produce green fluorescence (Cabantous et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation of split GFP technology and its properties.

claim: The binding between GFP11 and GFP1-10 is irreversible.
source: Since the binding between GFP11 and GFP1-10 is irreversible, it is possible that the reconstituted GFP::RPS-18 is not fully functional in contexts where ribosome activity is locally required or sensitive to dosage.
evidence: Statement about the irreversible nature of split GFP assembly.

claim: The reconstituted GFP::RPS-18 may not be fully functional in contexts where ribosome activity is locally required or sensitive to dosage.
source: Since the binding between GFP11 and GFP1-10 is irreversible, it is possible that the reconstituted GFP::RPS-18 is not fully functional in contexts where ribosome activity is locally required or sensitive to dosage.
evidence: Speculation about potential limitations of the RIBOS approach.

claim: Recent work in mice has shown tissue-type heterogeneity of ribosome composition.
source: Recent work in mice has shown tissue-type heterogeneity of ribosome composition (Simsek et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation of recent research on ribosome heterogeneity.

claim: Rpl38 knock-out mice show tissue-specific patterning defects, due to selective reduction on translation of mRNAs for some Hox genes.
source: Rpl38 knock-out mice show tissue-specific patterning defects, due to selective reduction on translation of mRNAs for some Hox genes (Kondrashov et al., 2011; Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation of research on functional consequences of ribosomal protein loss.

claim: In C. elegans not all ribosomes may contain RPS-18.
source: It is possible that in C. elegans not all ribosomes contain RPS-18, and therefore, that our approach may tag only a subset of ribosomes.
evidence: Speculation about potential limitation of the RIBOS approach based on ribosome heterogeneity.

claim: UNC-16 is a member of the conserved JIP3 proteins.
source: UNC-16 is a member of the conserved JIP3 proteins (Byrd et al., 2001).
evidence: Citation establishing protein family membership.

claim: JIP3 proteins act as an adaptor between cargos, for example mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) components, and kinesin.
source: These proteins act as an adaptor between cargos, for example mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) components, and kinesin (Koushika, 2008; Whitmarsh, 2006).
evidence: Citation of known function of JIP3 proteins.

claim: unc-16 was originally isolated by its uncoordinated movement and later shown to display mislocalized synaptic vesicles.
source: In C. elegans, unc-16 was originally isolated by its uncoordinated movement and later shown to display mislocalized synaptic vesicles (Byrd et al., 2001).
evidence: Citation of previous characterization of unc-16 mutants.

claim: In cholinergic motor neurons, UNC-16 was found to restrict membranous organelles, such as Golgi and endosomes to cell bodies.
source: In cholinergic motor neurons, UNC-16 was found to restrict membranous organelles, such as Golgi and endosomes to cell bodies (Edwards et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation of previous research on UNC-16 function.

claim: UNC-16 regulates distribution of a large molecular complex, ribosomes.
source: Our data show that UNC-16 regulates distribution of a large molecular complex, ribosomes.
evidence: Conclusion from genetic analysis of unc-16 mutants.

claim: UNC-16 localizes to the proximal axon in mechanosensory neurons.
source: Since UNC-16 localizes to the proximal axon in mechanosensory neurons (Edwards et al., 2013), these results might imply that UNC-16 restricts the ribosomes into the soma at the proximal axon.
evidence: Citation of previous localization data for UNC-16.

claim: UNC-16 might restrict the ribosomes into the soma at the proximal axon.
source: Since UNC-16 localizes to the proximal axon in mechanosensory neurons (Edwards et al., 2013), these results might imply that UNC-16 restricts the ribosomes into the soma at the proximal axon.
evidence: Inference from localization data and mutant phenotype.

claim: Both EM studies and biochemical evidences show that ribosomes can interact with microtubules.
source: Although both ribosomes and microtubules are well characterized cellular components, the connection between them has not been well appreciated. Both EM studies and biochemical evidences show that ribosomes can interact with microtubules (Suprenant, 1993; Suprenant et al., 1989).
evidence: Citation of previous research on ribosome-microtubule interactions.

claim: Microtubule disruption by nocodazole treatment makes ribosomes move into the neurites in chicken sensory neuronal cultures.
source: Microtubule disruption by nocodazole treatment makes ribosomes move into the neurites in chicken sensory neuronal cultures (Baas et al., 1987).
evidence: Citation of previous research on microtubule disruption effects.

claim: In C. elegans mechanosensory neurons, the number of growing microtubules increases three hours after axon injury, followed by consistent microtubule growth.
source: In C. elegans mechanosensory neurons, the number of growing microtubules increases three hours after axon injury, followed by consistent microtubule growth (Ghosh-Roy et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation of previous research on microtubule dynamics after injury.

claim: Fewer numbers of microtubules were observed at the injury site by EM.
source: We also observed fewer numbers of microtubules at the injury site by EM.
evidence: EM observation of microtubules at injury site.

claim: Mitochondria observed at the cutting site may locally supply energy for translation and microtubule dynamics.
source: Mitochondria observed at the cutting site may locally supply energy for translation and microtubule dynamics.
evidence: Speculation about the function of mitochondria at injury site.

claim: Microtubules restrict the ribosomes into the neuronal soma in unstressed conditions in mature neurons.
source: These data are consistent with a hypothesis that microtubules restrict the ribosomes into the neuronal soma in unstressed conditions in mature neurons.
evidence: Hypothesis based on genetic and drug treatment data.

claim: In neuronal soma, ribosomes are dynamically exchanged between two states: free in the cytosol or bound to the ER.
source: In neuronal soma, ribosomes are dynamically exchanged between two states: free in the cytosol or bound to the ER (Jan et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation of previous research on ribosome dynamics in soma.

claim: The balance between ER-bound and free ribosomes is important because in nascent polypeptide-associated complex (NAC) mutants in C. elegans, ribosomes are mistargeted to the ER, resulting in disrupted protein homeostasis.
source: The balance between ER-bound and free ribosomes is important because in nascent polypeptide-associated complex (NAC) mutants in C. elegans, ribosomes are mistargeted to the ER, resulting in disrupted protein homeostasis (Gamerdinger et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation of research showing importance of ribosome localization balance.

claim: Mislocalization of ribosomes in microtubule mutants may suggest that microtubules are components to prevent mistargeting ribosomes in the soma.
source: Mislocalization of ribosomes in microtubule mutants may suggest that microtubules are components to prevent mistargeting ribosomes in the soma.
evidence: Speculation about microtubule function based on mutant phenotypes.
